segments.vo: You have an idea for an app. Auth and a database in Supabase, done in an afternoon.
Then it needs live search. That means a SerpApi key, and a key can't live in the browser.
So keep it where your data already lives.
SerpApi, as Postgres functions.
Install it once.
One function call. Live Google results, as typed rows.
Underneath is a foreign data wrapper, written in Rust and compiled to Wasm, running inside Postgres. It reads the key from Vault, makes the call, and turns JSON into typed columns.
Every engine is generated from one catalog. Eight with typed columns, and any other SerpApi engine through one generic function.
Your app calls it the way it calls everything else in Supabase.
A static page, with no backend of its own. One request, real results, and the key never reaches the browser.
And it comes with the parts you'd otherwise have to build.
Anonymous visitors are refused.
Signed-in users get a daily quota. Twenty searches each, by default.
Hourly and monthly caps live inside the wrapper,
and they fail closed, before the request is sent.
Identical searches are normalised, so repeats hit SerpApi's own cache.
And every result keeps its search ID. Replay it from the archive, as rows or as Markdown, for thirty-one days. Free.
Scheduled search usually means a cron server, a worker, and somewhere to keep the results. Here, it's one line of pg_cron.
Every night at two-thirty, it runs inside the database. No servers to schedule.
For example, a nightly price history. The results land in a table, next to your own data, for as long as you want to keep them.
It installs from a release URL. On Supabase, or on your own Postgres. Same wrapper, same SQL.
Here it is on plain Postgres. Same function, same rows.
So any app on Postgres can put SerpApi in front of its users, safely.
Search is just another query. serpapi_fdw. Open source, built in Bengaluru.
